text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's German newspapers:
- German cabinet approves plans for changes to sick benefits for government employees including home visits to employees who call in sick and requiring a doctor's note from the first day of illness.

- Deputy parliament speaker Hans-Ulrich Klose presents report on speaker Rita Suessmuth to parliment committee about whether she used military aircraft for her private use. Committee due to discuss report on Thursday.
- Finance Minister Theo Waigel aims for upper tax rate of 39 percent and lowest tax rate around 20 percent or slightly under, in line with plans by a tax reform commission.
- Federation of German Industry (BDI) president Hans Olaf Henkel says reform in Germany is too slow and chances for new jobs have shrunk.
- BDI president Henkel says unemployment can be halved in Germany by year 2000, but rejects higher value-added tax to sink social contributions.
- The city of Hamburg sells more than a quarter of its stake in the Hamburgische Elektricitaets-Werke AG (HEW) electricity company for around 1.3 billion marks.

- German cabinet opens the way for the privatisation of the remaining 36 percent stake of national airline Deutsche Lufthansa AG, but shares fall in response to plans requiring Lufthansa ordinary shares to be converted to stock with restricted transfer rights.
- Unions ready to compromise over whether higher value-added tax (VAT) should be used to offset income tax reform or additional labour costs.
- The association of health insurers says contribution increases are possible.
- Prosecutors ask for almost seven years jail for the father of women's tennis number one Steffi Graf for tax evasion.
- The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) want the state to subsidise labour costs to enable unemployment to be cut.
- Cabinet approves changes to sick benefits for government employees.
- Federation of German Industry (BDI) president Henkel says two million new jobs are not "a utopia".
